title: dynamic-imports
description: Learn about dynamic-imports. Master the concepts, patterns, and best practices.

data.text: Dynamic imports enable JavaScript modules to be loaded on demand rather than at initialization. The import() function returns a promise that resolves to the module, enabling code splitting, lazy loading, and performance optimization.
Static vs Dynamic Imports

Static imports (import) load modules at initialization and are included in the initial bundle. Dynamic imports (import()) load modules at runtime when needed, enabling better performance through lazy loading.

data.title: Import Comparison

data.text: Dynamic Import Syntax
The import() function returns a promise that resolves to a module namespace object. It can be used with async/await or .then() syntax.

data.title: Dynamic Import Patterns
data.content: Different ways to use dynamic imports.

data.text: Dynamic Import Use Cases
1. Route-Based Lazy Loading
Load route components only when the user navigates to that route. This is the most impactful use case for dynamic imports.

data.title: Route Lazy Loading
data.content: Load routes dynamically with React Router.

data.text: 2. Component Lazy Loading
Load heavy or rarely used components only when they're needed. This is useful for modals, charts, rich text editors, and other complex UI components.

data.title: Component Lazy Loading

data.text: 3. Conditional Feature Loading
Load features based on user permissions, device capabilities, or user preferences. This avoids loading code that won't be used by the current user.

data.title: Conditional Feature Loading

data.text: 4. Prefetching for Performance
Combine dynamic imports with prefetching to load modules during idle time before they're needed. This reduces perceived latency when the user actually needs the functionality.

data.title: Prefetching Dynamic Imports

data.text: Webpack Magic Comments
Webpack supports magic comments that control chunk naming, prefetching, preloading, and other loading behaviors for dynamic imports.

data.title: Webpack Magic Comments

data.text: Error Handling and Fallbacks
Dynamic imports can fail due to network issues, missing files, or other errors. Always implement proper error handling and fallback UI.

data.title: Error Boundary for Dynamic Imports

data.text: Performance Considerations

items: Dynamic imports add HTTP overhead - use for larger modules (>20KB)
Prefetch likely-next modules to reduce perceived latency
Avoid dynamic imports for very small modules (overhead outweighs benefit)
Consider network conditions when deciding what to lazy load
Provide loading states and error handling for good UX
Measure performance to ensure dynamic imports provide actual benefit

data.title: Over-Lazy Loading Risks
data.text: Don't lazy load everything. Critical above-fold content should be in the initial bundle. Over-lazy loading can hurt performance by adding too many HTTP requests.

terms.definition: JavaScript's import() function that returns a promise, enabling runtime module loading.
Loading resources only when they're needed, rather than loading everything upfront.
Special comments in dynamic imports that control webpack's chunk naming and loading behavior.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Dynamic imports enable on-demand module loading for better performance
import() returns a promise that resolves to the module namespace
Use for route-based loading, component lazy loading, and conditional features
Combine with prefetching to reduce perceived latency
Webpack magic comments control chunk naming and loading behavior
Implement error handling and fallbacks for robust UX
Measure performance to ensure dynamic imports provide benefit
data.takeaway: Dynamic imports are essential for modern web performance, enabling code splitting and lazy loading while maintaining excellent user experience.
